prolfqua - a comprehensive R package for Proteomics Differential Expression Analysis

The R package contains functions for analysing mass spectrometry based experiments. It is intended for proteomics core facilities and researchers who analyse label-free protein or peptide intensities quantified with MaxQuant, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, FragPipe or similar software. This package is developed at the FGCZ. The package documentation including vignettes can be accessed at https://fgcz.github.io/prolfqua/index.html

prolfqua makes easy things easy while remaining fully hackable.

At its centre is a factory, build_contrast_analysis(): one call fits a model per protein and computes the requested contrasts. The method argument selects one of 20 models, and every model returns its results through the same interface. Start with the Introduction to prolfqua.

Statement of need

Label-free quantification (LFQ) experiments measure thousands of proteins or peptides in few samples, and values go missing more often at low intensity. Methods for their differential expression analysis are spread over packages with different input formats, model specifications and outputs (limma, DEqMS, MSstats, msqrob2, proDA, limpa), which makes it hard to choose a method for a dataset or to compare methods on it.

prolfqua gives these methods one data model, a long table with an AnalysisConfiguration naming the column roles; one model specification, R’s formula interface including mixed models; and one output format. build_contrast_analysis() fits any of its 20 methods and returns contrasts with the same columns, so a core facility can run, compare and report them in one workflow, and a researcher can check how much a result depends on the method. prolfqua also covers the steps around the test: quality control, normalisation, aggregation of peptides to proteins and sample-size estimation.

How to install prolfqua?

prolfqua requires R (>= 4.6); check your version with R.version.string and update R first if needed.

prolfqua is part of Bioconductor from release 3.24. To install the Bioconductor release:

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("prolfqua")

If BiocManager reports that prolfqua is not available for your Bioconductor version, update Bioconductor with BiocManager::install(version = "3.24") and run BiocManager::install("prolfqua") again.

Bioconductor publishes a release every six months. The development version on GitHub has the changes made since then, listed in the changelog. Installing it from GitHub needs the remotes package:

install.packages(c("BiocManager", "remotes"))
BiocManager::install("fgcz/prolfqua")

packageVersion("prolfqua") shows which version you have installed.

Some methods and plots use packages listed under Suggests; prolfqua asks to install them when they are needed.

Let us please know about any installation problems or errors when using the package: https://github.com/fgcz/prolfqua/issues

How to get started

How to build a LFQData object from a table with protein or peptide quantification results, and a table with sample annotation is described in more detail in the Importing your data vignette.

A minimal example for a table with protein abundances is:

# Table with abundances
df <- data.frame(
  protein_Id = c("tr|A|HUMAN", "tr|B|HUMAN", "tr|C|HUMAN", "tr|D|HUMAN"),
  Intensity_A = c(100, 10000, 10, NA),
  Intensity_B = c(NA, 9000, 20, 100),
  Intensity_C = c(200, 8000, NA, 150),
  Intensity_D = c(130, 11000, 50, 50)
)
# Table with sample annotation
annot <- data.frame(
  Sample = c("Intensity_A", "Intensity_B", "Intensity_C", "Intensity_D"),
  Group = c("A", "A", "B", "C")
)

# convert into long format
table_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(df, dplyr::starts_with("Intensity_"), names_to = "Sample", values_to = "Intensity")
table_long <- dplyr::inner_join(annot, table_long, by = "Sample")
# peptides per protein and sample; used as weights by some methods (1 if unknown)
table_long$nr_children <- 1L

# create the AnalysisConfiguration
config <- prolfqua::AnalysisConfiguration$new()
config$file_name <- "Sample"
config$work_intensity <- "Intensity"
config$hierarchy[["protein_Id"]] <- "protein_Id"
config$factors[["Group"]] <- "Group"

# Build LFQData object
analysis_data <- prolfqua::setup_analysis(table_long, config)
#> creating sampleName from file_name column
#> no qValue column specified in the data. Creating column qValue and setting qValues to 0.
lfqdata <- prolfqua::LFQData$new(analysis_data, config)
lfqdata$hierarchy_counts()
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   protein_Id
#>        <int>
#> 1          4

Once you have created an LFQData you can use prolfqua like this.

library(prolfqua)

## here we simulate peptide level data
startdata <- sim_lfq_data_peptide_config()
lfqpep <- LFQData$new(startdata$data, startdata$config)

## transform intensities and aggregate peptides to proteins
lfqpep <- lfqpep$get_Transformer()$log2()$robscale()$lfq
lfqpep$rename_response("log_peptide_abundance")
agr <- lfqpep$get_Aggregator()
lfqpro <- agr$aggregate()
lfqpro$rename_response("log_protein_abundance")

## plot Figure 3 panels A-D
pl <- lfqpep$get_Plotter()
panelA <- pl$intensity_distribution_density() +
  ggplot2::labs(tag = "A") + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none")
panelB <- agr$plot()$plots[[1]] + ggplot2::labs(tag = "B")
panelC <- lfqpro$get_Stats()$violin() + ggplot2::labs(tag = "C")
pl <- lfqpro$get_Plotter()
panelD <- pl$boxplots()$boxplot[[1]] + ggplot2::labs(tag = "D")
gridExtra::grid.arrange(panelA, panelB, panelC, panelD)

## specify contrasts
Contr <- c(
  "AvsCtrl" = "group_A - group_Ctrl",
  "BvsCtrl" = "group_B - group_Ctrl",
  "BvsA" = "group_B - group_A"
)

## fit a model per protein and compute the contrasts, here with limma
fa <- build_contrast_analysis(lfqpro, "~ group_", Contr, method = "limma")
#> fit (limma): 4 missing responses dropped (e.g. 7cbcrd~5725, 9VUkAq~4703, CGzoYe~2147): NA response (missing observation) left out of the fit
#> See $provenance().
head(fa$get_contrasts())
#> # A tibble: 6 × 16
#>   modelName estimate_type protein_Id  contrast    diff        FDR
#>   <chr>     <chr>         <chr>       <chr>      <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 limma     observed      0EfVhX~0087 AvsCtrl  -0.0506 0.485     
#> 2 limma     observed      7cbcrd~5725 AvsCtrl   0.707  0.00000378
#> 3 limma     observed      9VUkAq~4703 AvsCtrl  -0.593  0.00000378
#> 4 limma     observed      BEJI92~5282 AvsCtrl   0.273  0.0146    
#> 5 limma     observed      CGzoYe~2147 AvsCtrl  -0.231  0.00391   
#> 6 limma     observed      DoWup2~5896 AvsCtrl   0.266  0.00391   
#> # ℹ 10 more variables: std.error.unmoderated <dbl>, df.unmoderated <dbl>,
#> #   std.error <dbl>, statistic <dbl>, p.value <dbl>, sigma <dbl>, df <dbl>,
#> #   conf.low <dbl>, conf.high <dbl>, avgAbd <dbl>

## volcano plot
fa$get_Plotter()$volcano()$FDR

Design

The package for proteomics label free quantification prolfqua (read: prolevka) evolved from scripts written at the FGCZ to visualise and analyse mass spectrometry data; some of them are still in the R packages quantable, protViz and imsbInfer.

prolfqua stores the data in one table in long format, with an AnalysisConfiguration naming the column roles: the hierarchy (for example protein and peptide), the explanatory factors, the sample and the response. Data in long format, as written by Spectronaut, Skyline or DIA-NN, needs only this configuration; wide matrices, as written by MaxQuant, are converted with lfqdata_from_wide(), and the prolfquapp package reads the output of common quantification software. Results are data frames, so dplyr and ggplot2 work on every step.

Models are specified with R’s formula interface, including lme4 formulas for mixed models, so parallel, factorial and repeated-measurement designs need no special code. On top of the model fits, prolfqua implements p-value moderation as in limma, the peptide-median aggregation of PECA and ROPECA, and refits at the limit of detection for groups without observations, which makes these methods comparable within one framework. Besides differential expression, prolfqua computes coefficients of variation, estimates sample sizes, summarises missing values and intensity distributions, aggregates peptides to proteins (top N, Tukey’s median polish, robust regression) and compares models with likelihood ratio tests.

To use prolfqua, knowledge of R’s regression model infrastructure is an advantage.

Related projects

  • prolfquabenchmark - a package to document the performance of prolfqua, MSstats, msqrob2, and proDA. See documentation: https://prolfqua.github.io/prolfquabenchmark/
  • prolfquapp: Generating Dynamic DEA Reports with the prolfqua R Package https://github.com/prolfqua/prolfquapp
  • prophosqua - (scripts for the analysis of phospho experiments) https://github.com/prolfqua/prophosqua

Related packages

  • limma and DEqMS: moderated t-tests on a protein matrix; prolfqua’s limma, limma_voom and deqms methods call them
  • limpa: detection probability curve and precision weights; prolfqua’s limpa methods call it
  • PECA: peptide-median aggregation (PECA, ROPECA); prolfqua’s ropeca_nested is derived from it
  • MSstats: protein summarisation and linear mixed models
  • msqrob2: robust ridge regression on peptide or protein level, built on QFeatures
  • proDA: probabilistic dropout model, inference without imputation
  • DAPAR and DAPARdata: imputation and statistical analysis behind the Prostar interface
  • Triqler: Bayesian error propagation from identification to quantification (Python)

R packages to compute contrasts from linear and other models

  • marginaleffects Compute and plot predictions, slopes, marginal means, and comparisons (contrasts, risk ratios, odds ratios, etc.) for over 70 classes of statistical models in R.
  • emmeans Obtain estimated marginal means (EMMs) for many linear, generalized linear, and mixed models.
  • lmerTest computes contrast for lme4 models
  • multcomp computes contrast for linear models and adjusts p-values (multiple comparison)
